newsitem.title: UK: North Sea oil to lead supply surge in 1997.
newsitem.headline: North Sea oil to lead supply surge in 1997.

text.p: A wave of new oilfields in British and Norwegian waters will lead a surge in non-OPEC supply in 1997, washing away memories of a less than sparkling performance this year, economists and market analysts say.
Latin American, African and Asian non-OPEC producers also are expected to pump more crude next year.

Global oil production outside the 11-strong Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) should rise by up to four percent next year after technical setbacks and bad weather held back growth in 1996, the analysts said.

In its latest monthly report, the Paris-based International Energy Agency (IEA), which monitors oil market trends for members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), said non-OPEC supply would average 45.6 million barrels per day (bpd) versus 43.6 million bpd this year.

Other analysts were more cautious. The Washington-based Petroleum Finance Company (PFC), for example, said it expected supply from non-OPEC countries to run at 43.7 million bpd against 42.4 million in 1996.
While forecasts of the scale of growth vary, analysts agree the major North Sea producers will be fuelling the rise in non-OPEC output.
NORTH SEA TO SET PACE

"Firming up of the timing and production levels for several U.K. and Norwegian 1997 field developments and positive exploration and development experience in offshore areas around the world have reinforced the view that non-OPEC supply growth next year will be at the high end of the 1.5-2.0 million bpd range," the IEA said.

North Sea oil production will increase next year by seven percent over 1996 to average a record 6.47 million bpd, a 400,000 bpd hike based on rising supply from Norway, Britain and Denmark, according to a recent forecast by Edinburgh-based consultants Wood Mackenzie.
Seventeen new fields in the British and Norwegian sectors would more than offset the impact of biannual maintenance shutdowns and dwindling output from mature fields, they said.

"The past year has been a disappointing one for oil production in the U.K. from the point of view that new record output was not achieved as anticipated... Following a flat 1996, U.K. oil production in 1997 is forecast to renew the upward trend of the early 1990s," Wood Mackenzie said.
LATIN AMERICA FOLLOWS

PFC expects almost half the global growth -- or about 700,000 bpd -- to come from the North Sea, but Latin American producers, notably Mexico, Brazil and Colombia, will add another 300,000 bpd, senior economist Mohammed Abduljabbar told Reuters.
Five new floating production units are due onstream in the Campos Basin off Rio de Janeiro during 1997, taking Brazilian production above the record 900,000 bpd achieved in early November.
"(Brazilian) prospects beyond 1997 are even brighter, with several new finds...reported last month," the IEA said.

Mexican crude production is expected to top three million bpd next year, and in the absence of major terrorist activity, completion of the new Oceansa Pipeline around the middle of 1997 should lift Colombian production. RUSSIAN, U.S. SLIDE TO SLOW

Non-OPEC countries in Asia, Africa and the Middle East are also expected to contribute a combined 400,000 bpd in 1997 but equally significant will be the stabilisation of production in Russia and the United States, industry sources said.
The Russian government is expecting production to decline by two to three percent in 1997 from around 6.1 million bpd (305 million tonnes) this year, but the age of sharp falls are over.
"We expect to see production start to stabilise towards the back end of the year," said Stephen O'Sullivan, associate director of MC Securities Ltd.
Leading producers like LUKoil and Tatneft should begin reaping the rewards of restructuring and heavy investment.

Strong oil prices should also help slow the decline in U.S. domestic output next year, Independent Petroleum Association of America (IPAA) said recently. Last month, the IPAA, which represents 5,000 exploration and production companies accounting for about half U.S. oil output, forecast U.S. domestic oil supply to fall by 1.3 percent to 6.39 million bpd, mirroring a similar decline this year.
DEMAND TO KEEP PACE
Robust non-OPEC supply growth will have little market impact, however, with demand forecast to rise by almost two million bpd next year.

Assuming a 1.5 million bpd increase in non-OPEC output and continuation of the U.N. oil-for-food deal under which Iraq has signed contracts to export about 500,000 bpd, the supply-demand balance will be broadly stable.

"(Non-OPEC growth) will not be at a level to keep pace with steadily rising world oil demand, thus allowing room for any return of Iraqi oil to the market in 1997 with limited impact on oil prices, assuming no increase in current OPEC production quotas," Wood Mackenzie's Steve Scullion said.
